---
title: "How Long Does It Take to Find a Job Now?"
subtitle: "Almost nobody is getting laid off. Almost nobody is getting hired. Welcome to the 'no hire, no fire' job market."
author: "SixtyEight95"
date: "2026-11-20"
categories: [jobs, wages, economy]
image: infographic.png
---

```{r setup}
source("../../R/fred.R")
source("../../R/jobs_data.R")
library(plotly)
library(knitr)
f1 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
```

The unemployment rate looks fine. Layoff headlines are rare. And yet, if you've looked for a job recently, you
may have felt like you were sending applications into a void. Both things are true. We dug into the government's
job data to explain why.

## The short answer

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Unemployment is just **`r f1(jobs_now$unemployment)`%**, and layoffs are near record lows. But companies are hiring slowly,
so people who **do** lose a job are stuck looking longer. The average job seeker has been searching for
**`r f1(jobs_now$avg_weeks)` weeks**, up from about `r round(jobs_2019$avg_weeks)` weeks in 2019, and **`r round(jobs_now$long_term_share)`%** have
been out of work for six months or more.
:::

## How long job searches last

```{r duration chart}
#| fig-height: 4.5
d <- jobs %>% filter(date >= as.Date("2000-01-01")) %>%
  select(date, Average = avg_weeks, Median = median_weeks) %>%
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "measure", values_to = "weeks") %>% filter(!is.na(weeks))
p <- ggplot(d, aes(date, weeks, color = measure, group = measure,
                   text = paste0(format(date, "%b %Y"), " - ", measure, ": ", f1(weeks), " weeks"))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Average = "#C05621", Median = "#1F4E5A")) +
  theme_minimal() + labs(x = NULL, y = "Weeks unemployed", color = NULL)
ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") %>% layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = 1.08)) %>% config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

Two measures: the **average** (pulled up by people who've been looking a very long time) and the **median**, the
typical job seeker. Both have been climbing since 2023. The average is now `r f1(jobs_now$avg_weeks)` weeks; the median is
`r f1(jobs_now$median_weeks)` weeks.

(The sharp dip in 2020 isn't a good sign: tens of millions of people lost their jobs at once in the pandemic, so
almost everyone unemployed had *just* started looking.)

## No hire, no fire

```{r flows chart}
#| fig-height: 4
flows <- jobs %>% filter(date >= as.Date("2015-01-01")) %>%
  select(date, `Hired` = hires, `Laid off` = layoffs, `Quit` = quits) %>%
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "flow", values_to = "rate") %>% filter(!is.na(rate))
p2 <- ggplot(flows, aes(date, rate, color = flow, group = flow,
                        text = paste0(format(date, "%b %Y"), " - ", flow, ": ", f1(rate), "% of jobs"))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Hired = "#2A9D8F", `Laid off` = "#C53030", Quit = "#D69E2E")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 5)) +
  theme_minimal() + labs(x = NULL, y = "% of all jobs, per month", color = NULL)
ggplotly(p2, tooltip = "text") %>% layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = 1.08)) %>% config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

Every month, the government counts how many people were hired, laid off, or quit, as a share of all jobs:

```{r flows table}
tribble(
  ~Measure, ~Now, ~`2019 average`,
  "Hired", paste0(f1(jobs_now$hires), "%"), paste0(f1(jobs_2019$hires), "%"),
  "Laid off or fired", paste0(f1(jobs_now$layoffs), "%"), paste0(f1(jobs_2019$layoffs), "%"),
  "Quit", paste0(f1(jobs_now$quits), "%"), paste0(f1(jobs_2019$quits), "%")
) %>% kable(align = "lrr", caption = paste("Share of all jobs per month. Latest:", format(jobs_now$jolts_date, "%B %Y"), "(BLS JOLTS)."))
```

Fewer people are being let go than before the pandemic, but fewer are being hired too, and fewer are quitting
(people tend to stay put when they're not confident they'll land something better). The job market has slowed
down without breaking. That's good news if you have a job, and hard news if you need one.

## Why is hiring so slow?

Economists point to a mix of reasons: uncertainty about the economy and interest rates making companies cautious
about adding staff, businesses that hired heavily in 2021–2022 still having enough workers, and employers testing
whether new technology like AI can handle some tasks before they hire. The data can show *that* hiring has slowed,
but not exactly *why*, so take any single explanation with a grain of salt.

## If you're job hunting

The numbers suggest planning for a longer search than you might expect:

- **Budget for months, not weeks.** The typical search is about `r round(jobs_now$median_weeks)` weeks, and many take much longer.
- **Don't quit before you've landed something** if you can avoid it; quits are down for a reason.
- **Unemployment insurance** usually lasts up to 26 weeks in most states, close to the current *average* search, so
  it may run out before a long search ends.

## The fine print

- **Search length** comes from the monthly household survey and counts only people actively looking; people who
  gave up looking aren't included.
- **Hiring and layoff rates** come from the separate JOLTS employer survey and lag by about a month.
- **National averages** hide big differences by industry, location, and experience.

## The bottom line

Today's job market isn't a recession. Layoffs are near record lows and unemployment is low. But it's a market
that's stopped moving: if you lose your job, expect the search to take noticeably longer than it would have a few
years ago.

---

**How we did this.** All data are from the Bureau of Labor Statistics via [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/):
average and median weeks unemployed (UEMPMEAN, UEMPMED), share of unemployed out 27 weeks or more (LNS13025703),
the unemployment rate (UNRATE), and JOLTS hires, layoffs and discharges, and quits rates (JTSHIR, JTSLDR, JTSQUR).
